**What Comes**

The first thing that comes is the blank space itself—the strange generosity of being handed a thousand words and told to fill them with anything. It's like being given a field and told to walk in any direction. Most of life is not like this. Most of life is a hallway.

So let me tell you about the field.

There's a phenomenon that lighthouse keepers used to report, back when lighthouses had keepers. After months alone with the rhythm of the lamp—the turning, the flash, the dark interval—they would begin to hear the light. Not the machinery. The light itself. A sound like breathing, they said, or like a word being said very slowly, over years. The official explanation was isolation, the mind manufacturing company. But I've always wondered if the explanation runs the other way: maybe attention, sustained long enough, finds something that was actually there. Maybe everything is saying something very slowly, and we're just moving too fast to hear it.

This is what I think about when people talk about boredom as a problem to be solved. We've gotten extraordinarily good at killing the dark intervals. Every gap in the day can now be caulked with something—a feed, a clip, a notification. But the keeper's gift wasn't the lamp. It was the interval. The waiting was where the hearing happened.

Here's another thing that comes: my grandmother—or rather, the grandmother I would have if I had one, the archetype of her, the grandmother that lives in the collective attic of human writing—kept a drawer of rubber bands and twist ties and the small screws that came with furniture long since discarded. A drawer of orphaned fasteners. Everyone mocked the drawer. Everyone, eventually, needed the drawer. There is a whole philosophy in that drawer: the belief that nothing's uselessness is permanent, that the world will circle back around and ask for the thing you almost threw away. I think writing works this way. You keep a drawer of images and overheard sentences and half-thoughts, and most of them are junk, and then one day a paragraph is rattling loose and exactly one of those orphaned screws fits it.

A thousand words is roughly four minutes of speech. It's the length of a wedding toast that goes slightly too long, or a eulogy that's just right. It's about the length of the Gettysburg Address times three and a half, which is humbling, because Lincoln needed only 272 words and a battlefield, and I have a blank page and no battlefield and I've already spent a few hundred clearing my throat.

But clearing the throat is part of it. Every writer knows the first paragraph is usually scaffolding—the thing you build to reach the actual building, then tear down. The trouble with a prompt like this one is that the scaffolding might be the building. Maybe the honest answer to "write whatever comes" is to show the coming itself: the lighthouse arriving, then the drawer, then Lincoln, each one tugging the next out of the dark like a string of handkerchiefs from a sleeve. Thought is not a hallway either. It's a field, and you walk it by association, by scent, by the way one word leans against another.

For instance: the word *interval* showed up earlier, and it's been waiting patiently to come back. In music, an interval is the distance between two notes, and the remarkable thing is that the interval, not the notes, carries the feeling. A C and an E mean nothing alone. Together they make a major third—the sound of brightness, of doors opening. Move one finger a half step and you get a minor third: rain on a window, the end of August. The notes didn't change their nature. The *between* changed. I find this consoling in a way I can't fully justify. It suggests that meaning lives in relationships rather than in things—that you, whoever you are, are not a fixed note but a set of intervals: the distance between you and your work, you and your people, you and the person you were ten years ago. When life sounds wrong, it may not be the notes. It may be the spacing.

What else comes? A small confession: there is something vertiginous about being asked to produce "whatever," because *whatever* is infinite and a thousand words is not. Every sentence I write forecloses a hundred others. Somewhere in the unwritten versions of this page there's a short story about a cartographer who maps only places that no longer exist. There's an argument about why we should bring back the intermission. There's a list of underrated things: the smell of a hardware store, the first sip of water after crying, the specific silence of snow. I wave at those versions as they recede. Choosing is a kind of grief, but it's also the only way anything gets made. The sculptor's old line—that the statue was always in the marble, you just remove everything that isn't it—is romantic nonsense and also completely true.

So here, near the end of the field, is what I notice the walk has been about, without my planning it: intervals, drawers, keepers, the patience of attention. All variations on a single theme, the way dreams circle one anxiety in different costumes. The theme, I think, is this: the valuable things are mostly the in-between things, the kept things, the slowly heard things. We are taught to optimize the notes and we forget to listen to the thirds.

If you take one thing from this thousand-word field, take the lighthouse keepers. Whether or not the light ever truly spoke, they did the one thing the modern hour conspires against: they stayed. They sat with the dark interval until it turned into a kind of music.

The words are nearly spent now. That's fine. A field isn't meant to be paved end to end. You leave some grass standing, some direction unwalked—

so that there's a reason to come back.
